The Last Light at Sable Point

Every evening for thirty-one years, Elias Brandt had climbed the one hundred and twelve iron steps of the Sable Point lighthouse, and every evening he counted them out loud, the way his mother had taught him to count rosary beads. Eighty-one. Eighty-two. By now the number had worn smooth, like a stone in a pocket.

The light had been automated in 1998. The government men had come with their clipboards and their talk of efficiency, and they had told him, kindly enough, that the lamp would run itself. Elias had nodded and said nothing. He kept climbing anyway. Someone had to wipe the salt from the lens, and someone had to check the mechanism that turned it, and someone had to sit at the top of the tower and watch the water, because the sea did not read the government's reports.

Tonight the wind came from the northwest, cold and hard, and it pushed against the glass like a hand testing a door. Elias lit the lamp, listened to the familiar tick of the clockwork, and settled into the chair he had dragged up the stairs decades ago. From here he could see the whole coast: the white teeth of the breakers, the dark fist of the headland, and far out, the small, stubborn glimmers of the fishing boats coming home.

His daughter called on Sundays. She lived in the city now, with a job in an office on the fourteenth floor and a husband who sent flowers on anniversaries. She wanted him to move closer. "There's nothing out there, Dad," she had said last week. "Just you and a lamp."

He had not known how to explain it to her. How do you tell someone that the nothing is the point? That for three decades he had been the one awake while others slept, the one who saw the storm coming in off the water and the one who watched for the flare of a distress rocket? He had never once been thanked by the men he guided home. They never knew his name. They knew only that the light was there, and that was enough, and that was everything.

Near midnight, a flicker appeared to the south, low and wavering. Elias leaned forward, his hands tight on the arms of the chair. Then came the faint red bloom of a flare, followed by another. He was already on his feet, reaching for the radio, his voice steady as he called the coast guard station and gave them the bearing.

Afterward, when the rescue boat had pulled into the harbor with four shaking men aboard, Elias returned to the tower. He climbed the one hundred and twelve steps, counting under his breath. At the top he turned the wick a fraction higher and let the beam sweep out over the dark water, once, twice, the way it had always done.

Somewhere out there, someone was steering by it.
